info.title: HoneyBook API
info.description:
The HoneyBook API lets you read and write the data behind a HoneyBook account — contacts, projects, workspaces, smart files, tasks, notes, conversations and more.

It is a JSON HTTP API. Every request is authenticated with an OAuth 2.0 access token, every response is JSON, and every endpoint lives under a single versioned base path.

### Base URL

```
https://api.honeybook.com/api/v3
```

The version is part of the path. A new major version gets its own path and its own documentation; endpoints in `v3` are not removed or changed in place.

### Making a request

Send the access token as a bearer token:

```bash
curl https://api.honeybook.com/api/v3/contacts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <access_token>"
```

### How this documentation is organized

**Guides** describe the conventions that apply across the whole API. Read Errors, Pagination and Filtering & Sorting once and they apply to every endpoint you touch.

**API Reference** documents every endpoint, grouped by the resource it belongs to.

### Conventions worth knowing before you start

-   **Identifiers are opaque strings.** An id is a 24-character hexadecimal string. Treat it as an opaque token: do not parse it, and do not assume any structure or ordering.
-   **Timestamps are ISO 8601** in UTC, for example `2026-08-11T14:30:52Z`. Date-only fields are `YYYY-MM-DD`.
-   **Money is an object**, not a bare number — an amount together with its currency. Never assume a currency.
-   **Unknown query parameters are ignored, not rejected.** A misspelled filter name does not produce an error; it simply does not filter. Check your parameter names against the reference when a list returns more rows than you expected.
-   **Absent is not the same as empty.** A field that was not requested and a field that is genuinely empty are distinguished — see Relation Includes.

The API is private. To get access, fill in the [Request Access form](#tag/request-access).

tags.description: The HoneyBook API is currently private. Please submit this form to apply for access. ### How registration works HoneyBook registers applications itself; there is no self-service sign-up. Once your application is registered you receive a `client_id`, the issuer URL and your granted scopes. **No client secret is ever issued**: your application proves who it is with a key pair instead, as the [Authentication](#tag/authentication) guide explains. To register your application, HoneyBook needs: - A **JWKS URL** (HTTPS) that publishes your public key. - Your exact **redirect URIs** (HTTPS, no wildcards). - The **scopes** your integration needs, least-privilege. - An **engineering contact** and a **security contact** email. The form asks for these in its _Registering your application_ section. If you are approved, HoneyBook uses them to generate your OAuth client.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description:
The HoneyBook API is authenticated with **OAuth 2.0**, using the authorization code flow with PKCE. Your application never handles a HoneyBook password; the account holder signs in to HoneyBook directly and grants your application a scoped, revocable access token.

### HoneyBook is not the authorization server

This is the single most important thing to understand before you start, because it determines where your requests go.

HoneyBook operates the **API** and the **sign-in and consent screens**. The OAuth endpoints themselves — `/authorize`, `/token` and token revocation — are served by HoneyBook's identity provider on a **different host**.

| What you are doing                               | Where the request goes                      |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| Sending the account holder to authorize your app | `https://oauth.honeybook.com/oauth2/auth`   |
| Exchanging the code for tokens                   | `https://oauth.honeybook.com/oauth2/token`  |
| Refreshing an access token                       | `https://oauth.honeybook.com/oauth2/token`  |
| Revoking a token                                 | `https://oauth.honeybook.com/oauth2/revoke` |
| Calling the API                                  | `https://api.honeybook.com/api/v3/...`      |

There is no `/token` endpoint under `/api/v3`. Looking for one is the most common wrong turn.

### The flow

1. **Redirect the account holder to the authorization endpoint** with your `client_id`, your registered `redirect_uri`, the scopes you need, `response_type=code`, a `state` value, and a PKCE `code_challenge`.
2. **The account holder signs in to HoneyBook and reviews what you are asking for.** They see your application's name and a plain-language description of each scope, and they can decline any of them.
3. **HoneyBook redirects back to your `redirect_uri`** with an authorization code. Verify `state` matches what you sent.
4. **Exchange the code for tokens** at the token endpoint, sending your `code_verifier` and a `private_key_jwt` client assertion (see _Client authentication_ below — HoneyBook issues no client secret).
5. **Call the API** with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`.
6. **Refresh** with the refresh token when the access token expires. You only receive a refresh token if you requested the `offline_access` scope.

### Client authentication

To get a `client_id`, apply through the [Request Access form](#tag/request-access); HoneyBook registers your application and issues no client secret.

HoneyBook authenticates clients with **`private_key_jwt`** (RFC 7523), not a shared secret. You generate a key pair, publish the public key at an HTTPS JWKS URL you host (e.g. `https://your-domain/.well-known/jwks.json`), and prove your identity at the token endpoint by sending a short-lived `client_assertion` JWT signed with your private key. HoneyBook fetches your public key from that URL and verifies the signature — your private key never leaves your infrastructure. Rotating a key is self-serve: publish the new key at the same URL, no coordination needed.

Keys must be RSA or ECDSA — RS256/ES256 or stronger.

Redirect URIs must be HTTPS, with no wildcards, and are matched exactly — a trailing slash difference is a mismatch. You may send only one `redirect_uri` parameter per request.

PKCE is required on every authorization request, including for a confidential client like yours.

### Scopes

Scopes are granular and follow a `<resource>.<access>` shape: `projects.read`, `contacts.write`, and so on. The API's OAuth 2.0 security scheme lists every scope and what it grants.

Three scopes are required on essentially every integration and are not resource-specific:

| Scope            | What it is for                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `openid`         | Identifies the HoneyBook account that granted access.                                                                                                     |
| `honeybook.api`  | Permission to call the API at all. Necessary but never sufficient on its own — you still need the resource scope for whatever you are reading or writing. |
| `offline_access` | Issues a refresh token. Without it, access ends when the access token expires.                                                                            |

Ask only for what you need. The consent screen shows every scope you request, and a long list depresses the rate at which people complete authorization.

Writing implies reading, but not automatically: if you need to both read and write projects, request `projects.read` **and** `projects.write`.

### Which response means what

Authentication and authorization failures are deliberately not all distinguishable, and one of them will surprise you:

| Response                                                           | Meaning                                                                                       | What to do                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **401** with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"`      | The token is missing, malformed, or expired.                                                  | Refresh the token and retry once.                               |
| **403** with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"` | The token is valid, but was not granted a scope this endpoint requires.                       | Re-authorize with the additional scope. Retrying will not help. |
| **404**                                                            | Either the record does not exist, **or** it exists and this account is not allowed to see it. | Treat these as the same case.                                   |

That last row is intentional. The API will not confirm that a record exists to someone who is not entitled to it, so a permission failure is indistinguishable from a genuine miss. Do not write logic that infers existence from a 404.

tags.name: Errors
tags.description:
Every failure returns the same JSON shape, whatever went wrong. You can write one error handler and use it everywhere.

```json
{
    "error": true,
    "is_timeout": false,
    "error_type": "HBValidationError",
    "error_message": "title is missing",
    "error_data": {
        "fields": [{ "field": "title", "message": "is missing" }]
    }
}
```

| Field           | Notes                                                                                                                              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `error`         | Always `true` on a failure.                                                                                                        |
| `is_timeout`    | `true` only when the request exceeded the server's time limit. Safe to use as a retry signal.                                      |
| `error_type`    | A stable machine-readable identifier. Branch on this, never on `error_message`.                                                    |
| `error_message` | Human-readable. Wording may change at any time.                                                                                    |
| `error_data`    | Always present, `{}` when there is nothing to add. On a validation failure it carries a `fields` array naming each rejected field. |

### Status codes

| Status  | When                                                                                                                                                              | `error_type`                                                                        |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **400** | A parameter or filter failed validation, the request body was malformed, a business rule rejected the request, or the account's plan does not include the feature | `HBValidationError`, `HBBadRequestError`, `HBUserError`, `HBRestrictedFeatureError` |
| **401** | The access token is missing, malformed or expired                                                                                                                 | `HBInvalidJWTError`                                                                 |
| **403** | The token is valid but lacks a scope this endpoint requires                                                                                                       | `HBInsufficientScopeError`                                                          |
| **404** | The record does not exist — **or** it exists and you are not allowed to see it                                                                                    | `HBObjectNotFoundError`, others                                                     |
| **409** | The request conflicts with the current state, such as a duplicate or an illegal status transition                                                                 | `HBConflictError`                                                                   |
| **410** | The record existed and has been deleted                                                                                                                           | `HBObjectDeletedError`                                                              |
| **500** | Something went wrong on our side                                                                                                                                  | `HBInternalError`                                                                   |
| **503** | The endpoint is temporarily shedding load                                                                                                                         | `HBTempSuspendedRouteError`                                                         |

### Two behaviours that catch people out

**A permission failure returns 404, not 403.** If your token is valid but the record belongs to another account, you get a 404 that is byte-for-byte identical to the one you would get for an id that never existed. This is deliberate: the API will not confirm a record exists to someone not entitled to see it. The single exception is a missing OAuth scope, which returns 403 — there, the caller is known and the requirement is public.

**A 500 never names the underlying failure.** `error_type` is normalized to `HBInternalError` and the message is generic. If you need us to investigate one, capture the request path, the time, and any correlation headers on the response.

### Retrying

Retry on **500**, **503**, and any response where `is_timeout` is `true`, with exponential backoff. Do not retry **400**, **401**, **403**, **404**, **409** or **410** — the same request will fail the same way. A **401** is worth exactly one retry, after refreshing the token.

tags.name: Pagination
tags.description:
Every endpoint that returns a list is paginated, and they all use the same two parameters and the same envelope.

### Parameters

| Parameter  | Default | Limit                               |
| ---------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `page`     | `1`     | Pages are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed. |
| `per_page` | `25`    | Maximum **100**.                    |

```
GET /api/v3/contacts?page=2&per_page=50
```

### The envelope

A paginated response is always an object with `data` and `pagination`. It is never a bare array, so the response shape does not change when there are no results.

```json
{
    "data": [{ "id": "6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f01", "name": "Ada Lovelace" }],
    "pagination": {
        "page": 1,
        "per_page": 25,
        "total_items": 100,
        "total_pages": 4,
        "last_page": false,
        "offset": 0
    }
}
```

| Field              | Meaning                                                              |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `page`, `per_page` | Echo of what was applied, after defaults and clamping.               |
| `total_items`      | Total matching the query across all pages, not the number in `data`. |
| `total_pages`      | Total pages at the current `per_page`.                               |
| `last_page`        | `true` on the final page. Use this to end your loop.                 |
| `offset`           | Index of the first row in `data` within the full result set.         |

### Iterating a full list

Loop until `pagination.last_page` is `true`. Do not stop when `data` is shorter than `per_page` — that is also true of the last page, but checking the flag is unambiguous.

```
page = 1
loop:
  response = GET /api/v3/contacts?page=<page>&per_page=100
  process(response.data)
  if response.pagination.last_page: stop
  page = page + 1
```

Prefer a larger `per_page` over more requests. Fetching 1,000 records at `per_page=100` is ten requests; at the default it is forty.

### Deep pagination has a limit

Some list endpoints are backed by a search index that cannot page arbitrarily deep. Past roughly 10,000 records, they return **400** rather than failing partway through. If you need to walk a very large collection, narrow it with filters — by date range, by status, by owner — rather than paging further into an unfiltered list.

### Results can shift between pages

Pagination is a snapshot per request, not per traversal. If records are created or deleted while you are iterating, a record can appear on two pages or on none. When exactness matters, sort by a stable field such as `created_at` and filter to a closed time range so the underlying set cannot change beneath you.

tags.name: Filtering & Sorting
tags.description:
List endpoints are narrowed with flat, named query parameters. There is no query language and no operator syntax — each parameter has one fixed meaning, documented on the endpoint.

```
GET /api/v3/tasks
  ?status=open
  &due_after=2026-01-01
  &due_before=2026-06-30
  &assignee_ids=6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f01,6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f02
  &sort=-due_date,title
  &page=1&per_page=25
```

### How filters are named

The name tells you the comparison. You never write one.

| Shape                              | Meaning               | Example                    |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `<field>`                          | Equals                | `status=open`              |
| `<field>_after` / `<field>_before` | Inclusive range bound | `due_after=2026-01-01`     |
| `<field>_ids`                      | Matches any of a set  | `assignee_ids=<id1>,<id2>` |

A range is expressed as two separate parameters targeting the same field. Send `due_after` alone for an open-ended lower bound, `due_before` alone for an upper bound, or both for a closed range.

### Multiple values

A set parameter takes either a comma-separated list or the same key repeated. These are equivalent:

```
?assignee_ids=<id1>,<id2>
?assignee_ids=<id1>&assignee_ids=<id2>
```

Some set parameters also accept the literal token `none`, which matches records where the field is unset. Where it is supported, the endpoint's parameter description says so.

```
?workspace_ids=<id>,none
```

Different filters combine with AND. Values within one set parameter combine with OR.

### Sorting

```
?sort=-due_date,title
```

Comma-separated fields, applied in order as tie-breakers. A `-` prefix sorts descending; no prefix sorts ascending. Each endpoint documents which fields are sortable and what its default sort is.

### Two behaviours to be aware of

**An unrecognized parameter is ignored, not rejected.** `?stauts=open` returns unfiltered results with a 200, not a 400. This is standard for flat-parameter REST APIs, but it means a typo shows up as too many rows rather than as an error. When a list looks too broad, check your parameter spelling first.

**A recognized parameter with an unusable value is a 400.** `?due_after=not-a-date` fails immediately rather than being silently dropped.

**Enumerated filters list their allowed values** in the reference. Sending a value outside the list is not guaranteed to be rejected — depending on the field it may simply match nothing — so use the documented values.

tags.name: Relation Includes
tags.description:
Responses reference related records by id rather than embedding them. When you need the referenced record itself, ask for it by name with `include` instead of making a second request per row.

```
GET /api/v3/contacts?include=user,workspaces&max_workspaces=5
```

Nothing is populated unless you ask. This keeps the common case fast and makes the cost of a fat response something you opt into.

### The field is always there

An includable field is present in every response. Its **value** tells you what happened, so you never have to check whether a key exists.

|                               | Not requested | Requested, none exist              | Requested and found                   |
| ----------------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Single relation, e.g. `user`  | `null`        | `null`                             | `{ ... }`                             |
| Collection, e.g. `workspaces` | `null`        | `{ "data": [], "total_items": 0 }` | `{ "data": [...], "total_items": 7 }` |

An included collection is an object, not a bare array:

```json
{
    "id": "6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f01",
    "name": "Ada Lovelace",
    "user": { "id": "...", "first_name": "Ada" },
    "workspaces": {
        "data": [{ "id": "...", "name": "Spring wedding" }],
        "total_items": 7
    }
}
```

### `total_items` is how you detect truncation

`total_items` is the true number of related records for that specific parent — not the number returned. When `total_items` is larger than `data.length`, you hit your own limit and there are more. Fetch the rest from the related resource's own endpoint.

### Limiting a collection

Each includable collection has a `max_<name>` parameter, defaulting to **3**, with a maximum of **25**.

```
?include=workspaces&max_workspaces=10
```

The limit is per parent record, so it multiplies with `per_page`. `per_page=100&max_workspaces=25` asks for up to 2,500 nested records in one response — usually a sign you want the related endpoint directly instead.

A value outside the allowed range is a **400**, never a silent clamp.

### Rules

-   **Only one level.** `include=workspaces.project` is a **400**. To go deeper, make a second request against the related resource.
-   **`max_*` requires its `include`.** Sending `max_workspaces` without `include=workspaces` is a **400**, not a silently ignored parameter.
-   **Unknown include names are a 400.** Unlike filters, includes are validated — a typo here fails loudly.
-   **Each endpoint documents what it supports.** The set of includable relations differs per resource and is listed on the endpoint.

tags.name: Async Operations
tags.description:
Almost every endpoint completes within the request. A small number of operations do real work in the background — generating a document, calling a payment provider, processing an unbounded collection — and those return immediately with a task you poll.

You can tell them apart from the reference: an asynchronous operation is documented as returning **202 Accepted**.

### The pattern

**1. Start the work.** The operation returns `202` with a task:

```json
{
    "id": "6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f09",
    "task_type": "create_pay_link",
    "status": "pending",
    "result_resource_type": null,
    "result_resource_id": null,
    "failure_reason": null,
    "created_at": "2026-08-11T14:30:52Z",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-11T14:30:52Z"
}
```

**2. Poll for completion** at the single shared status endpoint, using the task's `id`:

```
GET /api/v3/async_tasks/6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f09
```

Every asynchronous operation in the API polls the same endpoint. There is one to implement, not one per feature.

**3. Fetch the result.** On success the task carries a **pointer**, not the result itself:

```json
{
    "status": "succeeded",
    "result_resource_type": "pay_link",
    "result_resource_id": "6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f10"
}
```

Read the finished record from that resource's own endpoint — here, `GET /api/v3/pay_links/6512a0b3f8d4c21a9e7b3f10`. The task never carries the result inline and never carries a URL, so the result is always fetched through a documented, typed endpoint you already know how to read.

### Status values

| `status`    | Meaning                                                        |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pending`   | Still running. Keep polling.                                   |
| `succeeded` | Done. `result_resource_type` and `result_resource_id` are set. |
| `failed`    | Terminal. `failure_reason` explains why. Do not keep polling.  |

`pending` means background work in flight and nothing else. A business state that merely sounds pending — awaiting payment, awaiting approval — is a different field with its own specific value.

### Polling advice

Poll with a short initial delay and back off — roughly one second, then two, then four, capping around thirty. Do not poll in a tight loop.

**Tasks do not live forever.** They are retained for a limited period after their last update and then removed. Polling a task past its retention returns **404**, so treat a 404 on a task you have not seen complete as an inconclusive result, not as a failure — check the target resource before retrying the operation.

**No result is delivered to you.** There are no webhooks or callbacks for task completion, and there is no `Location` header on the `202`. Polling is the only mechanism.
